newsitem.title: USA: Presidential race goes negative, U.S voters cry foul.
newsitem.headline: Presidential race goes negative, U.S voters cry foul.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
The U.S. presidential campaign is turning nastier with both sides stepping up their TV attacks, but voters increasingly say they are turned off by negative political advertisements.

In the past two weeks, both U.S. President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole have taken the gloves off in the air war. One Clinton spot managed to portray Dole simultaneously as old and callous while Dole has branded the president with the dreaded "L word", calling him a "tax-and-spend liberal."
According to an analysis by Kathleen Hall Jamieson at the Annenberg School for Communication, Republicans have run more attack ads than Clinton's Democrats in the past six months.
Some 63 percent of Republican spots have been "pure attack ads" while 88 percent of Democratic ads have been "comparative", making a case both against the opponent and for the sponsor.

Overall, the number of pure attack ads has fallen substantially so far this year compared to the 1992 election. That may be partly in response to growing evidence that voters are rebelling against overly negative politics.

In the campaign for the Republican presidential nomination earlier this year, millionaire publisher Steve Forbes peppered his opponents, including Dole, with a barrage of unrelentingly negative ads, until a vociferous voter backlash forced him to reverse his course.
Interviews with voters who took part in a Reuters opinion poll this week confirmed that many, especially women voters, were sickened by the whole process.
"I've seen too many campaign ads. I hate them tearing each other down. They should just talk about their issues," said Vivian Johns, a retiree from Mankato, Minnesota.
Some voters see Dole as being more negative than Clinton.

"I don't like Dole's back biting. He should let voters know what he stands for instead of what he thinks about Clinton," said Bea Harrison from Mesa, Arizona, who normally votes for Republicans but is still undecided this year.

Dawn Dooley, a homemaker from Dewey, Illinois, who voted Republican in 1992 but plans to support Reform Party candidate Ross Perot this time, said the ads just confused her and turned her off both major candidates.
"I'm sick of their ads. They just try to bash each other. I don't know what to believe any more," she said.
Some Republican voters believe Dole should be more aggressive in attacking Clinton's character.

"Dole is too nice. He should get out there and call a spade a spade. He should come down heavy, go for broke and tell the country what Clinton has done," said Bill Risner, a restaurant owner from Michie, Tennessee.

In past elections, negative ads have often proved extremely effective. They helped Republican George Bush destroy Democrat Michael Dukakis to win the 1988 election and have worked in countless congressional elections.

However, Dole's attacks on Clinton this year have yet to take hold. His latest spot, attacking Clinton's spending on "bigger government" and "wasteful projects" has had limited effect so far, according to the Reuters poll.
Asked if they agreed that Clinton was a "tax and spend liberal", 37.5 percent of respondents said they agreed while 50 percent disagreed.

In addition, many publications and television stations are now providing critical analysis of campaign ads, highlighting whether they contain falsehoods and distortions as well as discussing their strategic importance.
Hall Jamieson said the effect of this may be to increase voter cynicism, promoting voters' perceptions that "candidates are self-interested and running only for personal gain."
